corrections.caveats: First-party docs. The script is public (doc/source/reference/random/performance.py) and the page names GCC 9.3.0 (Linux) and MSVC 19 / VS2019 (Windows) on an AMD Ryzen 9 3900X, but optimization flags are not stated. Values are drawn in bulk (1,000,000 per call), so the per-value times amortize Python call overhead and do not represent one-at-a-time draws. The win depends on the platform: on 32-bit Windows the new generators are slower than MT19937 (overall PCG64 25, PCG64DXSM 39, SFC64 77 versus 100), and Philox scores 28 on 64-bit Windows. Not every distribution improves: Laplaces take 76.1 ns with PCG64DXSM versus 73.2 ns with MT19937 under Generator, and Laplace and Poisson gains are 3-27 percent. Much of the normals and exponentials gap versus RandomState comes from the algorithm (ziggurat versus Box-Muller and log inversion), not from the bit generator. PCG64 is the PCG family already catalogued as pcg-cpp, and SFC64 comes from PractRand, so those rows are partly evidence for the underlying algorithms. The baseline is NumPy's own C MT19937, not std::mt19937.

corrections.caveats: README benchmarks run by the author (benchstat, n=8-10) with CPU stated but no Go version or flags; the benchmark code is public in rand_bench_*_test.go. The win over math/rand/v2 is mixed: top-level Uint64 (+4.75%), Float64 (+7.92%), Intn (+2.58%) and Intn_Big (+15.35%) are slower than v2, and Rand_Seed goes from 0.57 ns to 46.09 ns (+7995%). The headline gains are in *Rand methods (float conversion, bounded ints, shuffle, perm) and against the legacy math/rand package. The roughly 99% gains against math/rand and x/exp/rand top-level functions on 48 threads come from lock contention on the global source; this package's top-level functions use goroutine-local runtime generators (wyrand via runtime.fastrand64 on most platforms), not sfc64. Go's own PCG source in math/rand/v2 is the closest named baseline. Go-only: not callable from C++. Files derived from Go's standard library are under BSD-3-Clause (LICENSE-go); the rest is MPL-2.0.

corrections.caveats: First-party documentation table. The script is public (doc/source/performance.py; also a top-level benchmark.py), and the CPU family is stated without a model name, but compiler and flags are not stated. Values are drawn in bulk (25,000 per call), so Python call overhead is amortized and the numbers do not represent one-at-a-time draws. On gammas, MT19937 under Generator (20.8 ns) beats PCG64 (23.2), PCG64DXSM (23.8), Xoshiro256 (22.1) and SFMT (21.5); only Romu variants and SFC64 (20.6) are faster there. The RandomState gap on normals and exponentials is inflated by Box-Muller and log-based inversion versus ziggurat in the newer code. The page itself recommends against all Mersenne Twister variants unless backward compatibility is needed. The baseline is NumPy's C MT19937, not std::mt19937. Dual-licensed NCSA or BSD-3-Clause; component licenses are stored with each component's source.
